title: automat evidence manifest
description: An append-only, hash-chained log of mutating operations. The chain of custody behind a 'born compliant' claim (DESIGN 11). Deliberately simple and ingestible by later systems.

id.description: Manifest identity. Per-account manifests use the account id.

genesis_sha256.description: records[0].record_sha256, copied into the header at the moment the first record is appended and never changed after. REQUIRED, not optional: an optional anchor is one that can simply be deleted, which is cheaper than the truncation it exists to catch — the same failure mode as an unsigned record (see records[].signature), where stripping the signature that would have caught tampering is cheaper than not tampering. Removing the front of a chain — records[0..k] — leaves a chain that still verifies, because previous_sha256 for the new first record can only be checked against ZeroHash, which the truncated record legitimately carries once it is treated as the new records[0]. genesis_sha256 catches this because record_sha256 already covers previous_sha256: re-anchoring a surviving record to ZeroHash changes its hash, so it can no longer match the anchor a second copy of the header holds. This does NOT close truncation against a full rewrite of the manifest, header included — the header sits outside every record_sha256 by design (see H4 in audits/AUDIT-2.md), because covering it would let a typo in created_at invalidate the whole chain. What this catches is a rewrite that keeps the ORIGINAL header while truncating records — detectable by anyone holding a second copy of that header, e.g. the management-side mirror DESIGN 11 describes.

records.description: Append-only. records[0].previous_sha256 is 64 zeros; every later record chains to its predecessor's record_sha256. A custody-transfer record ends the chain: at most one may appear, and nothing may follow it. This schema can express the 'at most one' half; that it is the LAST record is a chain-level invariant a validator must enforce, because JSON Schema cannot refer to an array's final position.

timestamp.description: RFC 3339 UTC timestamp, second precision, 'Z' suffix.

date.description: Calendar date, YYYY-MM-DD. Used only for effective dates, which are policy facts rather than event times.

prose.description: Human-supplied text. Control characters are forbidden: manifest fields are printed back in reports, and a newline in one of them can forge a line of that report. Written with \xNN rather than \uNNNN escapes, which are ECMA-262-legal but not accepted by every regex engine a consumer may validate with.

round_trip_id.description: An identity automat WRITES that a person is expected to read back and type — onto a command line, into a ticket, into a search box. Narrower than prose on purpose, and the reason is not injection: argument construction is the CLI's problem and stays there. This refuses to RECORD a value whose whole purpose is to travel through human hands into a shell. Two failure modes and the duller one is not the lesser: a value carrying a quote or a metacharacter is a record that suggests a different command than the one it appears to, and a value carrying whitespace cannot be selected by double-click, so the operator retypes it and gets it wrong. Used by manifest.id, records[].request_id, and custody_transfer.successor_manifest_id.

round_trip_ref.description: Same concern as round_trip_id, for identities automat does not mint and so cannot constrain to a plain id: an ARN, a KMS key id, a path-like reference. Admits the punctuation those forms actually require (colon, slash, plus, equals, at) and no more — in particular no whitespace, quote, backtick, dollar, semicolon, pipe, ampersand, or angle bracket. A KMS key ARN must round-trip through a `--key` flag unmangled; a value that could end a shell word must not. Bounded at 256 rather than the 2048 an ARN may formally reach, because Go's regexp engine caps a repeat count at 1000 and a bound the Go validator cannot express is one this schema must not express either — rule 8 is only meaningful if both layers state the same thing. 256 clears every real key reference with room to spare.

environment_profile_reference.description: The ENVIRONMENT profile in force for this operation, by id and content hash, plus the attestations over it that were VERIFIED at the time — never the ones merely present in the file. Named for the document type rather than just 'profile' because automat has three (environment, obligation, classification) and a record that says only 'profile' leaves the auditor to guess which kind of claim it is making. A record naming only the id is a record whose subject can be edited afterwards; the hash is what makes 'vended under this environment profile' a checkable claim rather than a label.

review_by.description: The environment profile's own review-by date, copied into the record. Copied rather than looked up because the point of an evidence record is to be readable years later without the inputs: an auditor reading this record can see that the environment profile behind it was already six months past review when the account was vended, without needing the file.

verified_signatures.description: The attestations over the environment profile that automat VERIFIED, as identity-and-role pairs. REQUIRED, and an EMPTY ARRAY IS THE NORMAL VALUE: automat performs no signature verification in v1, so it has nothing to put here and records the empty set. Required rather than optional so that an absent field cannot be read as 'unknown' — the distinction between 'nothing was verified' and 'the question was never asked' is exactly the one an evidence record must not blur, and the reader resolves which of those an empty set means from the record's own `tool_version`. Attestations present in the environment profile but unverified are deliberately NOT copied here: a record listing signatures it did not check would be a record that manufactures assurance out of a file's own claims about itself.

verified_signature.description: One attestation over an environment profile that verified — the identity and the CAPACITY it attested in, and nothing else. PROVENANCE ONLY: recording an attestation here says who stood behind the environment profile document, never that the environment profile is correct, applicable to this account, or approved for this use. The role is required alongside the identity so that the record cannot degrade into a bare list of names, which a reader would take for approval. What made the identity acceptable is an OPERATOR DETERMINATION against a trust policy the operator maintains; automat ships no trust anchor and no default accepted identity, so this field never means 'automat trusts this signer' — only 'this verified against the trust policy in force at the time'. automat is not a registry of signers and must never become one: it records what an operator's own trust policy accepted, and has no list of its own to consult.

role.description: The same closed vocabulary the environment and obligation profile schemas use. Roles exist so 'X authored this', 'Y adopted it', 'Z reviewed it' and 'the format validated' cannot collapse into one checkmark in a report generated from these records.

verified_against.description: The trust policy the operator's determination came from, by path or identifier, so a reader can ask what that policy said. Optional: v1 loads no trust policy and therefore has nothing to name.

is_custody_transfer.description: Matches a record whose operation is custody-transfer. Used only by the records[] uniqueness constraint; a chain may end once.

custody_transfer.description: Why and to whom custody of this manifest passed, and the artifact state at the moment it did. Required on a custody-transfer record and forbidden on every other kind, so a transfer cannot be smuggled onto an ordinary operation.

transferee.description: Who holds the chain from the effective date onward. Free text because the successor is often an organization or a role rather than an AWS principal — the transferring operator is already recorded in operator.arn.

effective_date.description: The date custody passes, which is a policy fact and may differ from the record's timestamp: the transfer is often agreed before, or recorded after, the moment it takes effect.

reason.description: Why the chain ends here. A chain that stops without a reason is indistinguishable from one that was truncated.

final_artifact.description: The control artifact in force at the moment of transfer, so the successor inherits a stated baseline rather than having to infer one from the whole chain.

successor_manifest_id.description: Identity of the manifest that continues the record, when the successor keeps one. Optional: a transfer out of automat's scope entirely has no successor manifest, and inventing one would be a false claim of continuity. The round-trip field with the longest fuse: the person who follows this pointer is a successor auditor years later, holding nothing but this record.

operator.description: The principal that performed the operation.

assumed_role.description: The role assumed to perform this operation, when brokered (DESIGN 5).

request_id.description: Vend request id. Ties records from a resumed run to the original request (DESIGN 7). The original round-trip field, and still the clearest case: a parked record exists precisely so an operator can read it weeks later and re-run `automat vend --resume <request-id>`.

artifact.description: The control artifact this operation enforced.

environment_profile.description: The environment profile this operation ran under: its id, its content hash, and the attestations over it that verified (an empty set in v1). Optional at the schema level because not every record has one behind it — `init` predates it and a custody transfer enforces nothing — but every record a `vend` writes carries it. Inside the record hash, so the environment profile a chain claims to have been vended under cannot be changed after the fact.

enforcement.description: What was actually attached or deployed.

error.description: Present when outcome is failure or parked. Carries the remediation text (CLAUDE.md rule 7).

action.description: The AWS action that was denied or failed.

remediation.description: What grant or change would fix this.

previous_sha256.description: record_sha256 of the preceding record; 64 zeros for the first.

record_sha256.description: SHA-256 over the canonicalized record with record_sha256 and signature omitted.

signature.description: Detached signature over record_sha256. The signer is an interface; a local key now, KMS later (DESIGN 11).

key_id.description: The key the record was signed by. A round-trip reference rather than a plain id because it may be a KMS key ARN, and because a key-id mismatch is REFUSED rather than reported as a bad signature — the remediation text tells the operator to supply the key the record names, so this value is one automat has actively asked a person to retype.

allOf.description: custody_transfer belongs to a custody-transfer record and to nothing else. Without the negative half, a transfer could ride along on an ordinary account-move record, where no reader would look for it. A transfer also carries no artifact, no enforcement, and no environment profile: it deploys nothing, and a second document reference beside custody_transfer.final_artifact leaves the reader to guess which one is the baseline being handed over.

outcome.description: A transfer that did not happen does not end a chain. Record the failure as the operation that failed; the chain continues.
